bodies.intuition: For every pixel in one frame, where did it go in the next? The answer is a dense field of little arrows, and it is the raw material for tracking, video compression, frame interpolation and stabilisation. It sounds like a matching problem and it is, but with a catch: a pixel on a smooth surface looks exactly like its neighbours, so matching alone cannot decide.
bodies.engineer: Modern methods build a correlation volume — every pixel of the first frame scored against candidate positions in the second — and then iterate a refinement over it rather than reading off the best match. Iteration matters because the first estimate is unreliable in exactly the regions where the appearance is ambiguous, and a few passes of refinement propagate confident matches from textured regions into flat ones.
bodies.math: Brightness constancy gives one equation per pixel and the flow has two components, so the problem is underdetermined at every single pixel — the aperture problem, and it is a statement about the data rather than about any method. Every approach therefore imposes a second constraint, historically a smoothness prior and now a learned one. The correlation volume's cost is the other half of the arithmetic: it grows as the square of the search radius, which is why nobody searches wide and everybody searches coarse-to-fine.
